About

Hello, I’m Maryam

Add About2.png

I’m a game designer and developer based in Amman, Jordan, working across gameplay systems, technical design and full-stack web development. Most of what I build starts as a question — what happens if power always costs something, or if the enemy you’re hunting can only be heard and never seen — and turns into a playable system that answers it.

I work mainly in Unity and C#, from the first line of a design document through prototyping, mechanics, balancing and polish. Alongside that I build web applications with JavaScript, Node.js, Python and MongoDB, which keeps me equally comfortable designing a combat loop and shipping a working product.

Outside of my own projects I teach game development to school students, work as a junior designer and developer for an international studio, and volunteer across Jordan’s gaming and tech community. I care most about ideas that are simple to understand and hard to put down.

Mission

I want to design games whose systems say something the story doesn’t have to.

What motivates me is the moment a player understands a mechanic without being told — when a rule they accepted five minutes ago suddenly becomes the reason they’re in trouble. I’m drawn to design where the meaning lives inside the systems: greed that compounds into debt, a machine you built yourself that you might lose, a room whose objects are pieces of someone’s identity.

What I want to contribute is that kind of design thinking to teams building ambitious games, and to the industry growing around me in Jordan and the wider MENA region. I’ve spent the last years learning in public — game jams, hackathons, competitions, teaching classrooms full of students their first line of C# — and I intend to keep opening that door behind me while I build games that are genuinely worth finishing.

Deal with the Devil

Every deal makes you stronger. Every deal takes something from you.

Unity · C#RoguelikeDesign & Development

Deal with the Devil is a fast-paced isometric hack-and-slash roguelike where the player fights through Hell to reclaim their sold soul. When pushed to the brink of death, the Devil offers powerful abilities in exchange for something fundamental to the player. Each deal provides a powerful advantage while introducing a hidden drawback, forcing the player to constantly weigh power against consequence.

The game’s progression revolves around an ever-growing debt. Every time the player sells more of their soul, the amount they must eventually repay increases, creating a cycle where greed makes the player stronger while simultaneously pushing the goal further away.

Play it

Widget blocked?Open on itch.io →

My Role

Game Designer & Developer

I was responsible for the project from concept through development, including the game’s design, programming, systems, balancing, environment layout, presentation, and project management.

What I Worked On

  • Designed the original game concept and core gameplay loop
  • Created and maintained the Game Design Document
  • Designed and implemented player movement and combat
  • Designed and implemented enemy behaviours and attacks
  • Created different enemy attack patterns and behaviours
  • Designed the Devil’s Deal system
  • Designed each deal around a balance between a powerful blessing and a meaningful curse
  • Worked extensively on game balancing and tuning
  • Designed the overall environment layout and room progression
  • Designed and implemented environmental hazards
  • Worked on post-processing and visual effects
  • Polished the overall game feel and moment-to-moment experience
  • Managed the project’s development and iteration

The Core Design

The central mechanic of the game is the Devil’s Deal. Instead of simply giving the player upgrades, every deal is designed as a trade. The player receives a powerful ability but gives up something in return.

The goal was to make every deal feel tempting while ensuring that its drawback could meaningfully change how the player approaches the game. This creates situations where the player may desperately want an ability while knowing that accepting it will make another part of the game more difficult.

The result is a progression system built around greed, sacrifice, and escalating debt.

The Idea Behind the Game

The idea for Deal with the Devil began through conversations with my younger sister, who reads a lot of books and often shares their stories with me. One particular story and its ideas about choices and consequences stayed with me and eventually became the starting point for this game.

Later, I participated in the Zanga 2025 competition, whose theme was Give and Take. Although I didn’t ultimately choose this idea for the competition, the theme helped the concept fully take shape. The idea of receiving something valuable while giving something meaningful in return became the foundation of the game’s core mechanic.

Since then, the concept has continued to evolve. Every time I pitched it to someone, their reaction made me want to explore it further. I kept asking myself how far the idea of a deal could be pushed and how the consequences could become part of the actual gameplay rather than simply part of the story.

Deal with the Devil became an opportunity to turn that idea into a complete gameplay system — where the player’s desire for power is also what makes their ultimate goal increasingly difficult to achieve.

Robocalypse

Build your robot from discarded junk. Trust your creation in battle — or lose everything you built.

Unity · C#Robot Building / CombatDesign & Development

Robocalypse is a robot-building combat game where players transform discarded components into custom machines and put their creations to the test in battle. Players gather parts from discarded materials and creatively assemble them into their own robots, giving them control over what they build and how they approach combat.

But every battle comes with a risk. Winning allows the player to take components from their opponent and use them to improve their robot. Losing means risking the components they fought to collect themselves. The game therefore turns the player’s own creation into something worth protecting, making every battle a test of both creativity and confidence.

Showcase

Video not loading?Watch on YouTube →

My Role

Game Designer & Developer

I was responsible for the game’s design and development, from the original concept and gameplay systems through implementation and iteration.

What I Worked On

  • Designed the original game concept and gameplay loop
  • Designed the robot-building and customisation system
  • Designed the component collection and progression system
  • Designed the risk/reward system around winning and losing components
  • Implemented player movement
  • Implemented combat mechanics
  • Implemented camera perspective switching
  • Designed and implemented environmental hazards
  • Designed the win and lose conditions
  • Worked on the overall environment and level layout
  • Designed the player experience and gameplay flow
  • Iterated on the game’s mechanics and balancing
  • Worked with my sister on the game’s 3D art and Blender-based assets

The Core Design

The core of Robocalypse is built around a simple question: how much do you trust the machine you created?

Players collect discarded components and use them to construct their own robot. Instead of receiving a predetermined character or loadout, the player creates their machine based on the parts they have available and the choices they make.

Those choices then have consequences in combat. Winning gives the player access to new components and allows their creation to grow stronger. Losing puts those components at risk.

This creates a progression system based on creativity, ownership, and risk. The more time and effort a player invests in their robot, the more meaningful the decision becomes to put it into battle.

The Idea Behind the Game

The idea for Robocalypse came from watching Bholi with my younger brother.

What inspired me most was seeing the character use creativity to solve problems and protect the environment. His gadgets were made from discarded and reused objects, turning things that would normally be considered garbage into something useful.

That idea stayed with me. I wanted to explore the same concept through a game where the player isn’t simply handed equipment. Instead, they collect discarded components and use their creativity to turn them into something new — a robot of their own.

From there, I wanted the environmental message to exist within the gameplay itself. Reusing discarded objects isn’t just part of the game’s story; it is the foundation of how the player progresses.

That eventually led to the game’s central risk: if you build something yourself, how much are you willing to risk it? Winning lets you salvage parts from your opponent and continue developing your machine. Losing means potentially losing the components you’ve collected. The environmental theme and the progression system therefore work together: something discarded can become valuable, and something valuable can be lost.

Collaboration

I handled the game’s design and development. For the 3D art, I collaborated with my sister, who has experience with Blender and assisted with the game’s visual assets.

Room Echoes

A ghost haunts a room filled with memories. You can’t see it — you have to listen for what it left behind.

Unity · 6DoF VRExploration / PuzzleDesign & Development

Room Echoes is a narrative-driven VR exploration and puzzle game where players enter a memory-filled room haunted by an invisible ghost. Unable to rely on sight alone, players must use sound, environmental clues, and spatial awareness to locate hidden memory objects and recover three out of five before the ghost makes them disappear. Once enough memories have been reclaimed, the player must confront the ghost directly and use a mystical blade to finally release it.

Showcase

Video not loading?Watch on YouTube →

My Role

Game Designer & Developer

I designed the game’s concept, VR experience, gameplay loop, interaction systems, and player experience, and implemented the core gameplay in Unity.

What I Worked On

  • Designed the original game concept and gameplay loop
  • Designed the VR experience around spatial awareness and heightened senses
  • Designed how the player explores and interacts with the room
  • Designed the memory-object collection system
  • Designed the ghost’s behaviour and interaction with the environment
  • Designed the sound-based system for locating the invisible ghost
  • Designed the clues the ghost leaves through its movement and interactions
  • Designed the ghost’s ability to make memory objects disappear
  • Designed the final sword encounter and ghost defeat mechanic
  • Implemented the gameplay and player interactions in Unity
  • Designed the overall pacing and player experience
  • Built the environment using Unity Asset Store assets

The Core Design

The central mechanic of Room Echoes is finding something you cannot see.

The ghost is completely invisible, forcing the player to rely on sound, spatial awareness, and environmental clues. Rather than simply searching an area until an enemy appears, the player has to investigate the room and interpret the information the ghost leaves behind.

The ghost itself also challenges the traditional portrayal of ghosts. Instead of being completely intangible and silent, it physically exists within the environment. It can collide with obstacles and produce sounds, allowing the player to gradually determine where it is.

At the same time, the player is racing against it. The ghost can pass through the memory objects and make them disappear, meaning the player must locate and recover enough memories before they are lost.

The Room as a Memory

One of the core ideas behind Room Echoes came from designing my own room.

While arranging it, I started noticing how many of the objects around me represented parts of who I was. Some reflected my interests, some carried memories, and others had sentimental value simply because of what they meant to me. The room started to feel like a physical representation of its owner.

In Room Echoes, the room is more than a level. Its objects are echoes of the person who once inhabited it. The memories attached to those objects are fragments of that person’s identity, while the ghost represents what remains behind. This is where the name Room Echoes comes from: the room contains echoes of a person who is no longer fully there.

The Idea Behind the Game

The concept came together from two experiences I was having at the same time: discovering VR for the first time and designing my own room.

When I first interacted with VR, I was surprised by how heightened my senses felt. Sounds became much more noticeable, the space around me felt tangible, and I became aware of details I would normally ignore in a traditional game. That made me wonder: what if a game made those senses the player’s primary tool?

The idea of an invisible ghost came from that question. Instead of simply seeing the enemy, the player would have to sense its presence.

I also wanted to challenge the way ghosts are normally portrayed in movies. They are often invisible or transparent, able to pass through objects without making much of an impact on the physical world. I wanted to reverse that relationship: the ghost would be invisible, but it would still physically interact with its surroundings and make sounds.

What Makes It Interesting

The core experience is a combination of hide-and-seek and detective work. The ghost is always hiding, but it continuously leaves clues through sound and its interactions with the environment. The player isn’t given its location; they have to investigate, listen, connect clues, and gradually narrow down where it is.

This creates a constant sense of anticipation. Every sound could be a clue, every interaction could reveal the ghost’s location, and the player is always racing against it to recover the memories before they disappear. That made Room Echoes one of the projects I genuinely enjoyed playing myself.

Technical Details

EngineUnity
Platform6DoF VR
GenreExploration / Psychological / Puzzle
Gameplay Time~20 minutes per level
Target AudienceAdults 18–35

Minecraft Education — HTU Digital Campus

A digital twin of a university, built so students could walk through their future.

Minecraft EducationRedstone & Command BlocksEducational Design

As part of a collaboration with Minecraft Education, we worked on creating educational experiences designed for students and children. The project that stood out to me most was the creation of a digital twin of our university inside Minecraft Education.

The goal was to give prospective students an interactive way to explore the university, learn about its unique academic system, visit different spaces, and interact with instructors through the Minecraft environment. This was particularly valuable because the university follows a different educational model from many other universities in Jordan and has introduced Game Development as a new career path.

Hay Day — Java

A farming game rebuilt from scratch, with no engine underneath it.

JavaNo EngineSystems & UI

Hay Day is a Java-based recreation of the farming game Hay Day, developed entirely from scratch without using a dedicated game engine. I built the complete game, including its core gameplay systems and a functional UI, entirely in Java.

The project was a significant technical challenge because implementing systems that a game engine would normally provide required extensive amounts of code and manual development. Building the game this way gave me a deeper understanding of what actually happens underneath a game engine — from managing game logic and UI to structuring and connecting the different systems.

More importantly, the project became a stepping stone toward my next stage of development: learning to work with professional game engines. After experiencing firsthand how much has to be built manually, I wanted to understand not only how to use an engine, but why engines are designed the way they are and what they abstract away. This gave me a much stronger technical foundation for engine-based game development.

Zeeh

Amman traffic, turned into the obstacle course it already is.

Amman Game JamUnityTeam Project

Zeeh was developed during the Amman Game Jam, where our team explored one of the most recognisable everyday problems in Jordan: traffic.

The game was inspired by Awda Bishifta, a locally known delivery game, and was designed as a potential second iteration that introduced a new core mechanic centred around traffic and vehicle movement.

The main gameplay twist was car bumping. Players had to push and manoeuvre other cars out of their way to create a path toward their destination. This turned the traffic itself into the main gameplay obstacle, transforming a familiar frustration into a simple but interactive game mechanic.

The project was developed under the constraints of a game jam, requiring us to quickly translate a real-world problem into a playable and understandable gameplay loop.

Qasr Amra — AR Heritage Experience

Heritage Hackathon project — 2nd place, national level.

UnityAugmented RealityHackathon

Qasr Amra is an augmented reality experience designed to make Jordan’s historical sites more engaging and meaningful to local visitors. The project addresses a common issue in local tourism: many people visit heritage sites without fully understanding their historical and cultural significance, making it harder to develop a genuine appreciation for them.

Our concept transforms a visit to Qasr Amra into an interactive AR experience. Visitors can use their device to explore the site while receiving real-time information about its architecture, symbols, and historical elements. AR overlays can explain the purpose of different structures, reveal how spaces were used, introduce the people who once lived there, and provide context for the artwork and icons found throughout the site.

Showcase

Video not loading?Watch on YouTube →

My Role — Unity & Technical Development

I was responsible for the technical side of the project, including the Unity development and the creation of the project video. I handled the implementation of the interactive experience and worked with the team to translate our design ideas into a functional technical concept.

While I focused on the Unity and technical development, the rest of the team worked across the research, design, presentation, and other competition requirements. We collaborated closely to ensure that the technical experience supported our overall goal: making Qasr Amra easier to understand, explore, and appreciate.

PageRank Search Engine & Visualiser

A miniature search engine that ranks the web it crawls.

PythonGraph AlgorithmsD3.js

Showcase

View the repositorygithub.com/maryamalkholi/Pythonrepo
View the repository →

Project Goal

To build a miniature search engine that can crawl webpages, analyse the connections between them, calculate their importance using the PageRank algorithm, and visualise the results.

What I Did

I developed a web-crawling and ranking pipeline in Python. I collected webpages and their links, stored the relationships between them, implemented the PageRank calculation through iterative processing, and generated the resulting data for an interactive visualisation.

Idea Behind the Project

The project models the web as a network of interconnected pages. Pages that receive links from other important pages are given greater importance, allowing the system to calculate a ranking for each page rather than simply treating all pages equally.

Key Features

  • Web crawler for discovering linked pages
  • Graph-based representation of webpage relationships
  • Iterative PageRank calculation
  • JSON data generation
  • Interactive D3.js network visualisation
  • Visual representation of page importance

Technical Focus

Python, web crawling, graph algorithms, PageRank, iterative algorithms, data processing, JSON, D3.js, and interactive data visualisation.
